Income-seeking investors often look to Singapore’s largest
real estate
giants for stability and consistent cash flow.
In October 2026, three major CapitaLand-managed trusts –
CapitaLand Ascendas REIT
(SGX: A17U), or CLAR,
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, and
CapitaLand India Trust
(SGX: CY6U), or CLINT – released their third-quarter (3Q2026) business updates.
Since all three trusts report full financial results on a half-yearly basis, these updates did not declare distributions per unit (DPU).
However, they offer a clear window into operational health, portfolio moves, and future growth drivers.
CLAR: Active Capital Recycling and Steady Operational Gains
CLAR holds an impressive portfolio of 236 properties valued at S$20.7 billion as at 30 September 2026.
In its 3Q2026 business update, CLAR did not disclose revenue or net property income (NPI), but operational metrics showed solid improvement.
Portfolio occupancy improved to 90.1%, up from 89.1% in the prior quarter, supported by newly acquired Singapore logistics assets and stronger leasing across its US logistics portfolio.
Rental reversions strengthened to 9.9% for the quarter, with Australia leading at 32.5%, lifting the rental reversions for the first nine months (9M2026) to 9.0%.
Management expects full-year rental reversions to remain in the high single digits.
Portfolio expansion remained active with acquisitions of 5 Tuas Avenue 5 for S$133.9 million and 25 Loyang Crescent for S$504.2 million, at initial yields of 6.6% and 6.9% respectively.
This brought total 9M2026 acquisitions to about S$1.8 billion.
To optimise its balance sheet, CLAR is divesting three Singapore properties for S$281.7 million at a 25% premium to valuation.
If the proceeds are used to repay debt, aggregate leverage would fall from 41.8% to about 41%.
Two redevelopments were newly announced: 29 International Business Park in Singapore (S$264.3 million, expected 1H2030) and Hawleys Lane in the UK (S$76.2 million, expected 2H2028).
These bring CLAR’s ongoing projects – a mix of developments, redevelopments and asset enhancements – to seven, worth S$847.7 million.
Management expects the development and redevelopment projects to deliver stabilised yields on cost of 6% to 8%.
Related articles:
STI Downturn: 3 Temasek-Linked S-REITs to Watch
CICT vs CapitaLand Ascendas REIT: Which CapitaLand Giant Is the Better Buy?
CICT: Major Portfolio Moves Drive Top-Line Growth
CICT is Singapore’s largest REIT, holding a S$28.7 billion portfolio across 25 retail, office, and integrated development properties.
For 3Q2026, gross revenue jumped 15.0% year on year (YoY) to S$464.5 million, while NPI rose 13.8% to S$334.9 million.
For 9M2026, gross revenue and NPI grew 10.0% and 10.4% YoY to S$1.3 billion and S$965.4 million, respectively.
Portfolio committed occupancy improved to 96.1%, accompanied by 9M2026 rental reversions of 4.6% for retail and 7.1% for office.
Top-line expansion was driven by the acquisition of Paragon on 1 July 2026, contribution from the enhanced Gallileo building in Frankfurt, and the step-up acquisition of CapitaSpring.
In 3Q2026, NPI for integrated developments surged 40.8% YoY to S$123.5 million, offsetting an 8.2% decline in retail NPI, which was partly due to the divestment of Bukit Panjang Plaza.
Operations stayed resilient, with 9M2026 shopper traffic up 2.3% and tenant sales per square foot rising 2.1%.
CICT completed the divestment of Asia Square Tower 2 (AST2) on 17 September 2026 for net proceeds of S$2.45 billion at an exit yield of 3.0%.
Asset enhancements remain on track: the S$24 million Tampines Mall upgrade wrapped up in 3Q2026, while a S$160 million enhancement at Plaza Singapura and The Atrium@Orchard targeting 6% to 7% returns has commenced.
Aggregate leverage stood at 39.7%, with the average cost of debt easing to 2.8%.
Related articles:
Keppel DC REIT vs CICT: Which REIT Would I Buy Today?
Unlocking CICT’s Growth Engine: From AEIs to a S$1.1B Hougang Expansion
CLINT: Local Operational Strength Tempered by Currency Headwinds
CLINT is a business trust that owns IT parks, industrial facilities, a logistics park and a data centre across five Indian cities, totalling 22.0 million square feet of completed space.
In Singapore dollar terms, gross revenue for 9M2026 fell 8% YoY to S$206.4 million, while NPI declined 6% to S$161.3 million.
However, these declines were driven by an 11% depreciation of the Indian rupee against the Singapore dollar.
In rupee terms, gross revenue and NPI actually expanded 2% and 4% YoY respectively.
Growth was boosted by higher income from existing properties and contributions from MTB 6 at International Tech Park Bangalore (ITPB), partly offset by lost income from divested assets CyberPearl and CyberVale.
Occupancy held steady at 91%, while trailing 12-month rental reversions reached a robust 23%.
CLINT is positioning itself for substantial multi-year growth, with its development pipeline set to expand total floor area by 46% to 32.2 million square feet by 2030.
Key projects include MTB 7 at ITPB (fully pre-committed to a Fortune 500 firm, completion 3Q2027), CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai (delivering 53 megawatts in 4Q2026), and six forward purchases valued at S$1.0 billion.
Gearing sits at 38.2%, with average debt cost at 5.7%.
Underlying market demand remains strong, as evidenced by record Indian office absorption of 66.4 million square feet in 9M2026.
Related articles:
4 REITs That Could Benefit from Singapore’s S$5B Equity-Market Push

Get Smart: Active Management Keeps the Engine Running
While macroeconomic uncertainties and
interest rat
e fluctuations remain key considerations for real estate investors, these CapitaLand entities continue to show why active management matters.
By selling lower-yielding or mature assets – such as CICT’s AST2 or CLAR’s Singapore properties – and reinvesting into higher-yielding developments and acquisitions, management teams are positioning their portfolios to capture long-term growth while keeping debt levels balanced.

shifts as we head into the year-end financial results.

title: Eurozone 3Q growth beats estimates despite slump in France
article:
(Oct 30): The euro-area economy grew at twice the pace analysts predicted, despite an unexpected slump in France and headwinds including elevated inflation and the selloff in bond markets.

Gross domestic product across the 21-member currency bloc rose 0.4% in the third quarter (3Q), Eurostat said on Friday. Performances were mixed among its biggest members as Germany and Spain grew, Italy stagnated and France shrank by 0.1%.

The overall outcome highlights Europe’s broader sturdiness, not just to the Iran war’s inflationary impact but to the heat waves and droughts that marred much of the summer. Still, the European Central Bank (ECB) has flagged downside risks and could yet hike interest rates for a third time in December after standing pat this week.

While inflation hasn’t spread beyond energy yet, officials in Frankfurt are wary. Separate data from Italy and France won’t reassure them, with prices jumping by 5.6% and 3.8% in October, the quickest since 2023 and ahead of expectations.

Inflation in Spain, despite easing a touch as anticipated, remained elevated at 4.9%.

See also: AI darling Taiwan extends economic growth run unseen since 1987

The jump in global bond yields is another drag, with France’s shaky fiscal and political position making it the region’s focal point. Its economy was already the euro area’s major laggard, only narrowly avoiding a recession in the first half amid soft domestic demand, falling investment and as hot weather hurt agriculture.

The outlook is bleak. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is in the midst of another parliamentary showdown over austerity, against a backdrop of social and political upheaval before presidential elections in 2027 where the far right leads polls.

“France’s economy is at a standstill due to a unprecedented convergence of external and domestic shocks,” Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Friday. “It needs to pick up. We need to restore confidence and for that having a budget is essential as that is what will allow us to bring down interest rates.”

See also: Lagarde downplays inflation risk as ECB holds, announces her early exit

German GDP rose 0.2% despite factors including low water levels in the River Rhine. A public-spending spree on infrastructure and defense is generating optimism while carmakers may benefit from a European cap on Chinese hybrid-vehicle imports.

At the same time, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made fresh efforts to perk up growth through social-welfare reforms and attempts to lure private capital.

“The headline overstates the strength of the economy. National data suggest Ireland accounted for about half of the increase, while the four largest economies grew by just 0.1% on average. With the conflict in Iran unresolved and energy prices still high, we think the bigger drag is yet to come. For now, though, the stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB remains on track for another 25bp rate hike in December,” says Simona Delle Chiaie, chief euro-area economist at Bloomberg Economics.

Italy’s government forecasts GDP will increase 1% in 2026, helping finance some of the tax cuts Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has promised before elections next year.

She’s also asked Brussels for extra leeway of about €28 billion for energy and defense outlays. Any slowdown in growth would complicate other fiscal commitments, including getting the budget deficit below 3% of output.

Spain, whose latest GDP reading was driven by domestic demand and trade, has shown significant resilience, with the central bank listing private consumption, job creation and population growth among drivers.

It sees growth of 2.6% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027, comfortably above the euro area’s pace. It’s largely shaken off political instability including Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez inability to pass a budget.

title: Bitcoin drops below US$77,000 as Binance hack shakes crypto
article:
(Oct 30): Bitcoin sank below US$77,000 ($98,383) for the first time in more than a month, deepening a sell-off after Binance Holdings revealed a record hack that rattled the crypto industry and renewed questions about the security of customer assets — even at the world’s largest digital-asset exchange.

The original cryptocurrency declined as much as 3.1% on Friday to fall as low as US$76,300. Other tokens, including some that were impacted by the security breach, also fell. Binance’s BNB token has declined about 5% over the past 24 hours to around US$700.

The breach — in which attackers siphoned off over US$6 billion — is the largest crypto theft on record, and delivers another blow to an industry that has spent years trying to shed its reputation for hacks, scams and exchange failures. It’s also putting Binance’s own defences under scrutiny by raising questions about how an exchange of its size — with more than US$135 billion of assets on its platform — could have succumbed to a breach of such magnitude.

Binance on Friday said that it has reserved US$6.34 billion of company funds in the wake of the incident.

“The broader crypto market was already leaning bearish, which is why the sell-off spread so quickly across the board,” said Jeff Ko, the chief analyst at ViaBTC. He added that Binance can absorb the losses.

See also: Record Binance hack shows no crypto firm is too big to breach

Bitcoin and other tokens were already under pressure this week with broader macro forces weighing on the market. Futures contracts for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 were down 2.4% ahead of the open following disappointing earnings reports from the likes of Amazon.com Inc and Intel Corp.

Bitcoin had hovered around US$80,000 for much of the week. However, a Friday expiry of US$11 billion worth of options on the platform Deribit loomed over the market, adding to the broader risk-off mood. About US$1.3 billion worth of bullish positions on cryptocurrencies were wiped out in a 24-hour period, according to Coinglass data.

“The downside is the series of body blows to crypto infrastructure over recent months could dissuade market entrants,” said Noelle Acheson, who writes the Crypto is Macro Now newsletter. “We have seen that self-custody isn’t safe, exchange custody isn’t safe, and the swarm of AI bot attacks on security in all online applications is going to make everyone even more nervous.”

See also: Binance says US$6.3 bil impacted as crypto reels from hack

The upside, however, is that “every new security breach does make security stronger”, she added.

title: China’s mega banks report profit jumps as margins recover
article:
(Oct 30): China’s mega banks reported their biggest quarterly profit increases in recent years as they reined in bad loans and interest margins recovered from record lows.

At Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd, the nation’s largest lender, profit in the third quarter rose 10% to 111.96 billion yuan. That was the biggest gain in five years.

Net income at Agricultural Bank of China Ltd rose 11% and Bank of Communications Co saw a rise of 10.1%. China Construction Bank Corp posted an 9.8% increase and Bank of China Ltd reported a 6.4% gain.

The performance suggests the worst of the profitability crunch may be behind the state commercial banking sector, which has spent years absorbing the financial costs of supporting a slowing economy and an ongoing real estate downturn.

State banks have played a central role as economic shock absorbers, trimming mortgage rates, extending credit to troubled property developers, and pumping loans into government-backed manufacturing and green energy sectors.

That mandate triggered sharp declines in net interest margins, driving industry-wide margins well below the 1.8% threshold historically viewed by regulators as necessary to sustain healthy capitalisation.

See also: PBOC reveals overnight rate at 1.25% before policy anchor shift

ICBC’s net interest margin (NIM), a key gauge of profitability, improved one basis point to 1.29%, after posting steep drops earlier.

Asset quality held largely steady across the major lenders, with bad-loan ratios remaining contained.

See also: BYD earnings dampen hopes Chinese car stocks will reverse rout

Beijing is providing another round of capital support for its state-backed financial giants, with the Ministry of Finance selling 300 billion yuan in special bonds to replenish core Tier 1 capital at eight institutions, including ICBC and Agricultural Bank. The two lenders plan to raise as much as 260 billion yuan combined, with the bulk provided by the ministry.

The move follows a 520 billion yuan recapitalisation in 2025, meaning all six of China’s biggest state lenders have now received support.

For China’s banking sector, the core challenge is pivoting from capital adequacy to capital productivity. Following years of rapid balance-sheet expansion and fresh rounds of state-backed recapitalisation, lenders must now prove they can convert thicker buffers into sustainable returns on equity without taking on outsized credit or market risk.

title: PBOC reveals overnight rate at 1.25% before policy anchor shift
article:
(Oct 30): China’s central bank announced the rate on its overnight reverse repurchase agreements is lower than its current seven-day benchmark, after unveiling plans to adopt it as the main policy lever.

The rate is currently 1.25%, compared with 1.4% on the current seven-day benchmark, according to a statement from the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) on Friday. While the PBOC hasn’t previously made public the rate at which overnight reverse repurchase agreements were conducted, it was set at 1.25% during the first such operation in June, Bloomberg News reported at the time.

The central bank will start to conduct overnight reverse repo operations every day starting from Nov 2, and reduce the frequency of its seven-day reverse repo transactions, it said. The latter will only be used during stretches such as tax payment times and end of month periods.

Earlier in October, the PBOC gave the clearest signal yet of plans to revamp its toolkit by shifting from the seven-day reverse repo rate to the overnight one. The move would be part of a decades-long effort to reform China’s interest-rate system from a centrally planned framework, and better align the PBOC with other major central banks.

Some analysts expected the switch in the main policy lever to take months, since the PBOC will likely need to gradually increase the frequency of the overnight liquidity operation.

title: Britain’s plan to tax its way out of debt tests the limits
article:
(Oct 30): Britain was singled out for praise by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) this month for the boldest deficit-reduction plan of any Group of Seven nation. Bolder still is its decision to deliver the whole squeeze with higher taxes, as economists warn that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is pushing the boundaries of what’s possible.

Over the five years of the current parliamentary term, the government plans to reduce borrowing by £76 billion (US$102 billion or $130 billion). All of that and more, £107 billion in total, will be done through tax hikes, the Resolution Foundation said in its analysis of Wednesday’s budget.

In 2010, the then-Conservative chancellor, George Osborne, split his austerity programme 80:20 between spending and tax as he sought to repair the public finances in the wake of the financial crisis. His Labour predecessor, Alistair Darling, had planned for a 66:34 division.

Healey is pushing the other way at a time when the tax burden is at its highest since the Second World War and living standards are under renewed assault, this time from the energy shock caused by the US-Iran conflict.

Analysis this month by Adam Slater, the lead economist at Oxford Economics, found that while all consolidation programmes have a high failure rate, “the evidence suggests that fiscal adjustments are more likely to succeed if they rely mainly on spending cuts rather than tax rises”.

See also: PM Burnham says he wants UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime

The budget raised taxes by roughly £6 billion a year from 2028 and topped up departmental day-to-day budgets by an average of £3 billion a year. On Thursday, Healey said there are no plans to bring down the hundreds of billions that Britain spends on welfare each year before the next general election, due in 2029.

The approach has opened up Labour to attacks from the opposition Conservative Party. “On the big challenges, what has this budget actually done? It does not reduce borrowing. Total debt has gone up. It does not properly fund defence,” said shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith. “It does not cut taxes to get the economy growing. Instead, they are putting up taxes again.”

His choice of tax levers suggested he is running out options. With his hands tied by Labour’s manifesto pledge not to raise any of the four main tax rates, much of the work was done through administrative tweaks, including powers to deduct funds directly from debtors’ bank accounts.

See also: Axel Springer to cut Telegraph jobs after buying UK newspaper

Additional taxes on savers, landlords and banks raised only £2 billion, and the increased bank surcharge is withdrawn after 15 months. Five of Healey’s measures have a “high degree of uncertainty”, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) judged.

Rodrigo Valdes, the director of the IMF’s fiscal affairs department, said earlier this month that the UK has raised taxes so much there is little left that does not have side effects. “More revenues is not easy,” he said. “It distorts at the end of the day.”

“There is a limit to how much you can squeeze out of households and businesses before crimping economic growth,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist of Capital Economics. “We may have reached that limit.”

Tax receipts climbed to 36% of gross domestic product (GDP) last year and are on course for 38.6% of GDP in 2031-2032, the OBR predicts. Between 1997 when Labour last took power and the eve of the pandemic in 2020, the burden averaged 32.7%. The bulk of the increase is coming through frozen tax thresholds, which have dragged millions of people into paying more tax as their pay rises. A full-time worker on the national minimum wage earning £25,275 is now halfway to paying higher 40% rate of tax.

Tax hikes since 2020 by both the former Conservative government and the current Labour one partly explain the collapse in living standards this decade, Resolution chief executive Ruth Curtice said. Real household disposable incomes are forecast to rise just 1.4% this decade, just a tenth of the growth in the 2010s which itself was the worst decade since at least the 1960s.

“The 2020s are on course to have the lowest growth in incomes of any decade on record,” Resolution’s post-budget report said, “because of rising taxes and import prices.”

Taxing the rich is no longer an easy option, with Bloomberg analysis last month showing that the share of total income tax paid by the highest earners in the UK has doubled in less than two decades — a hit of £100 billion. That comes on top of other raids targeting the wealthy on everything from private school fees and expensive houses to Britain’s long-standing non-domiciled regime.

Work by the Institute for Fiscal Studies in 2024 showed that the share of tax paid by the top 1% of income taxpayers rose from 25% in 2010-2011 to 28.5% in 2023-2024, while income and payroll taxes took a smaller fraction of the earnings of a single full-time median earner with no children than at any time for almost 50 years.

title: BYD earnings dampen hopes Chinese car stocks will reverse rout
article:
(Oct 30): BYD Co’s latest earnings signal that this year’s surge in car exports won’t be enough to recapture lost momentum in Chinese auto stocks.

Its shares slipped as much as 2.4% in Hong Kong on Friday after the country’s biggest carmaker reported third-quarter profits and revenue that missed analysts’ estimates, overshadowing overseas sales more than doubling from a year ago. An export-led growth story didn’t help BYD’s nearest local competitor, Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd, either as its stock fell for a second day.

The two auto giants’ failure to reinvigorate enthusiasm bodes ill for a once high-flying industry that investors have soured on for more than a year. China’s car market, the world’s largest, continues to shrink and more recently some authorities abroad have stepped up efforts to slow down the flood of Chinese imports.

“Exports face new headwinds just as they have become a key profit driver for BYD,” said Joanna Chen, an analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence. Investors will focus on how fast BYD can ramp up overseas production, and how profitably it can make cars overseas compared with back in China, she said.

Some companies, particularly foreign brands, have been even worse off. Volkswagen AG, Europe’s largest carmaker, on Thursday reported a loss for the latest quarter, largely because of exposure to China.

See also: China builds its GDP on competitive advantage

In the run-up to the earnings reports, signs emerged that some investors were turning more bullish on BYD as short sellers pared back bets against the stock, which has fallen nearly 30% in Hong Kong this year, heading for its biggest annual drop since 2011.

Profit climbed 28% from a year earlier but fell short of the average analyst estimate compiled by Bloomberg by 17%. Revenue was about 8% less than what analysts had estimated.

Scale gains were absorbed by cost pressures, according to a research note from analysts at Jefferies, who have a 'hold' rating on BYD shares.

See also: Geely's profit climbs as rising exports offset China slump

The results also pointed to a build-up of inventory, currency-related losses amid the continued appreciation of the Chinese yuan and a big drop in income from financial investments, the Shenzhen-based carmaker disclosed.

BYD and other Chinese carmakers are facing slowing demand and intense price competition domestically, making a pivot overseas — where their budget-friendly, technology-focused models make more money — critical to survival.

But their popularity is creating new hurdles, particularly in Europe, where Chinese automakers outsold Japanese rivals for the first time ever for a full quarter. Registrations of Chinese-branded cars roughly doubled to make up 12.7% of total sales across the region, led by hybrids, according to market researcher Dataforce. Five years ago, Chinese brands accounted for barely 1% of European sales.

The European Union has already imposed extra tariffs on China-made battery-electric vehicles, and this month agreed in principle to curb fast-growing imports of hybrid cars from China. Plug-in hybrid vehicles have accounted for nearly half of BYD’s passenger car sales.

The restrictions are spurring BYD to spend billions of dollars to build a physical presence in Europe. Its first factory in the region, located in Hungary, is set to start mass production in the fourth quarter, Stella Li, the executive vice-president who heads the company’s overseas business, said this month. France and Spain are on the shortlist for future plants, and the carmaker wants to build a European workforce of about 40,000 employees by the end of the decade, she said.

For the first nine months of the year, deliveries have lagged behind sales during the same period a year earlier, putting its annual sales target — five million to 5.5 million — further out of reach.

However, the company did see a recovery in deliveries at home as it ramped up production of its latest generation of Blade batteries, with August and September local shipments marking month-over-month increases.

The company is betting on the fast-charging system to further boost sales, and has brought the first sport utility vehicle equipped with the latest batteries to Europe during the Paris Motor Show. Li also confirmed earlier this month that BYD had ordered 10 more vessels, in addition to its operational fleet of eight cargo ships.

Yet domestic pressure is set to continue into next year. China’s total sales are set to tumble 22% this year to just 18.5 million vehicles, the Passenger Car Association estimates. The group expects average growth of 2% next year, a pace that it describes as a weak recovery rather than a strong rebound.
